course.name: Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II

question.text: For a surface $S$ given by $z = x^2y$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by \[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \Bigg( \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\, xy + \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,x^2 +R \Bigg) \: \textrm{d}A. \] From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A. \] Since our surface $S$ is of the form $z=x^2y,$ it can be parameterized as

\[ \mathbf{r}(x,y) = \left\langle x,\: y,\: x^2y \right\rangle. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x & = \left\langle 1, \: 0, \: 2xy \right\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_y & = \left\langle 0, \: 1, \: x^2 \right\rangle \end{align*}

Now, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_y &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & 2xy \\ 0 & 1 & x^2 \end{vmatrix} = \left \langle -2xy, \: -x^2, \: 1 \right \rangle. \end{align*}

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(x,y)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_y) \,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \langle P, \: Q, \: R \rangle \cdot \left \langle -2xy, \: -x^2, \: 1 \right \rangle \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \Bigg( \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\color{blue}-2P}\, xy + \left(\,\bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\color{blue}-Q}\,\right)\,x^2+R \Bigg) \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

example.title: Expressing Flux Over a Surface as a Repeated Integral Using a Formula

question.text: For a surface $S$ given by $x = k(y,z)$ for $(y,z) \in D,$ the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by \[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \Bigg( P- \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}} \,{\bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}}- R\,{\bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}} \Bigg) \: \textrm{d}A. \] From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A. \]

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $x = k(y,z),$ it can be parameterized as

\[ \mathbf{r}(y,z) = \left\langle k(y,z),\: y,\: z \right\rangle. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_y & = \left\langle \dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y}, \: 1, \: 0 \right\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_z & = \left\langle \dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z}, \: 0, \: 1 \right\rangle \end{align*}

Now, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_y \times \mathbf{r}'_z &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y} & 1 & 0 \\ \dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z} & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \left \langle 1, \: -\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y}, \: -\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z} \right \rangle. \end{align*}

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(x,y)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_y \times \mathbf{r}'_z) \,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \langle P, \: Q, \: R \rangle \cdot \left \langle 1, \: -\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y}, \: -\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z} \right \rangle \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \Bigg( P - \bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\color{blue}Q}\,\bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\color{blue}\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y} } - R\,\bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\color{blue}\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z} } \Bigg) \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

example.title: Expressing Flux Over a Surface as a Repeated Integral Using a Formula

question.text:
Calculate the flux of the vector field

\[ \mathbf F(x, y, z) = \left\langle y, \: x+z, \: 0 \right\rangle, \]

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=e^x$ for $-1 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A. \]

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(e^x) = e^x \\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(e^x) = 0 \end{align*}

In this case, the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ is given by \[ \iint\limits_S \left\langle y, \: x+z, \: 0 \right\rangle \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} \]

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf F(x,y,z){:}$

\begin{align} \mathbf{F}(x,y,g(x,y)) &= \left\langle y , \: x+z, \: 0\right\rangle \Big|_{z=e^x} \\[3pt] &= \big\langle \underbrace{y}_{P}, \: \underbrace{x+e^x}_{Q}, \: \underbrace{0}_R \big\rangle \end{align}

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \left\langle y, \: x+z, \: 0 \right\rangle \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D ( -y \cdot (e^x) - (x+e^x) \cdot 0 +0 ) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \big( -ye^x \big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} \big(-ye^x \big) \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} \left[ -\dfrac{y^2 e^x}{2}\right]_{y=0}^{y=1} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac 12 \int_{-1}^{1} e^x \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac 12 \left[ e^x \right]_{-1}^{1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{e^{-1} - e}{2} \end{align*}
